Design of experiments is the planning of which input settings to measure so that the effects of interest can be estimated efficiently and with known precision. Classical designs fix the set of runs in advance, from evenly spaced scans of one variable to factorial, Latin square and response surface designs that vary several factors at once. Model-based approaches such as active learning and Bayesian optimization choose runs sequentially using a surrogate model and its uncertainty, so the total number of experiments is not known in advance and a stopping criterion is needed.

## Designs on a remote instrument (2025)

In a tutorial on automating the Claude-Light instrument, Kitchin moved from a one-variable scan fit by linear regression, to a nine-run Latin square (generated with pycse) estimating the effect of three LED inputs on three photometer outputs, to a Gaussian process with a linear kernel fit to twenty runs and inverted with Nelder-Mead to hit target outputs ([Kitchin 2025](/papers/kitchin2025b/)). He notes that output scaling and a white-noise kernel were needed for sensible uncertainty, which matters because over- or underestimated uncertainty makes sequential designs either never finish or stop at the wrong answer. He argues that sequential designs keep the same loop structure as classical ones, as used in [self-driving laboratories](/papers/topics/self-driving-laboratories/). Summary: [kitchin2025b](/papers/kitchin2025b/).

## Model-driven plate design for surfactant mixtures (2025)

Chilkunda, Kitchin and Tilton used a physical model to place experiments for mapping the [critical micelle concentration](/papers/topics/critical-micelle-concentration/) of a binary surfactant mixture ([Chilkunda et al. 2025](/papers/chilkunda2025/)). After measuring the pure-component CMCs, they drew five constant-ratio lines through composition space and put trials where each line crosses the regular solution theory boundary predicted for seven interaction parameters between -6 and 0, plus two trials well below and one above to calibrate low and high fluorescence. Duplicating all but the top trial filled 95 wells of a single plate, concentrating samples near the expected boundary. Only a rough prior range for the interaction parameter is needed, and the authors suggest an iterative broad-then-narrow search when even that is unknown. See also [high-throughput experimentation](/papers/topics/high-throughput-experimentation/). Summary: [chilkunda2025](/papers/chilkunda2025/).
